title: CYSTINOSIS, LATE-ONSET JUVENILE OR ADOLESCENT NEPHROPATHIC TYPE

relationships.phenotype: CYSTINOSIS, LATE-ONSET JUVENILE OR ADOLESCENT NEPHROPATHIC TYPE

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that late-onset juvenile or adolescent nephropathic cystinosis, also called intermediate cystinosis, is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the CTNS gene.

checks.claim: Late-onset juvenile or adolescent nephropathic cystinosis is also called intermediate cystinosis.

checks.claim: Late-onset juvenile or adolescent nephropathic cystinosis is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the CTNS gene.
checks.evidence_quote: The disease occurs due either to the combination of one mild mutation and one which is known to cause nephropathic cystinosis or to homozygosity for a predicted mild mutation.
checks.explanation: Compound heterozygous or homozygous CTNS mutations (the gene is named in the title) cause intermediate cystinosis.

paragraphs.text: Thoene et al. (1999) found that intermediate cystinosis results either from one mild CTNS mutation combined with a mutation known to cause nephropathic cystinosis, or from homozygosity for a predicted mild mutation. This is consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance. Attard et al. (1999) described infantile nephropathic cystinosis, which is allelic with the late-onset form, as an autosomal recessive disease.

paragraphs.text: Attard et al. (1999) described 3 patients whose cystinosis began before 7 years of age but whose disease course was milder than the infantile nephropathic form. paragraphs.text: Thoene et al. (1999) described 6 patients with intermediate cystinosis who had mutations in the CTNS gene. Two of the mutations had not been described before. The disease resulted either from one mild mutation combined with a mutation known to cause nephropathic cystinosis, or from homozygosity for a predicted mild mutation. Transfecting cystinotic fibroblasts with either normal cDNA or a cDNA derived from a mutation causing intermediate cystinosis partly corrected their phenotype.

paragraphs.text: Attard et al. (1999) screened the CTNS gene in patients with infantile nephropathic cystinosis, patients with late-onset cystinosis, and patients whose phenotype did not fit the classical definitions. They found 23 different mutations, 14 of them novel. The mutations found in 2 patients with late-onset cystinosis affected functionally unimportant regions of cystinosin, which the authors said accounts for the milder phenotype.

paragraphs.text: Attard et al. (1999) studied 25 patients with infantile nephropathic cystinosis. Twelve had 2 severely truncating CTNS mutations, consistent with loss of functional protein. The other 13 had missense mutations or in-frame deletions that were predicted to disrupt transmembrane domains and cause loss of protein function. In contrast, the mutations in 2 late-onset patients affected functionally unimportant regions of cystinosin.
